lines.note: Mumon here means unpatterned, explained by aya nashi; it is a new entry anticipated by the previous page's catchword, not a continuation of the illiteracy sense. The scan aligns it with the headwords, so the provisional indentation is removed. Veſti continues without an added hyphen.

Completes the description of cloth or a garment without decorative work or painting. The small mark over the o of Mumõna is read as an abbreviation tilde, not the OCR caron; the adjective qualifies qirumono below.
Mumõna kirumono denotes an unpatterned garment. The Portuguese repeats the absence of ornament or painted decoration; qirumono is the historical Japanese form, not a defective kimono spelling.

runs.text: Eſteos, ou colũnas ſobre q̃ aſſen-

lines.note: Munabashira are supporting posts or pillars for the roof-ridge beam. The headword is aligned with the other entry starts, correcting the provisional indentation; Eſteos and the abbreviations colũnas and q̃ remain unexpanded.

runs.text: tão a traue da cumieira da caſa.

lines.note: Completes aſſentão and specifies the beam along the house's roof ridge. The line belongs to the pillar definition, not to Munacado below.
Munakado concerns the form of a doorway or the front of a house. The scan supports a contiguous fronteſpicio rather than OCR fronte ſpicio; the historical vowels and tilde placement are retained.
Da caſa completes the doorway/front-of-house explanation. This genuine short continuation remains its own physical row.
Munagai is the horse's breast strap or breastpiece. The equestrian context distinguishes it from the human armour term a few rows below.
Munagawara are roof-ridge tiles. The Portuguese cumieira links this entry to the preceding architectural vocabulary.
Munagi is the ridge beam itself. Unlike Munabaxira, it denotes the supported horizontal member rather than the posts beneath it.
Munaita is a breastplate, rendered as the chest-piece of armour. The source's joined darmas is retained without introducing an apostrophe or modern spacing.
Munamoto denotes the pit of the stomach or breast. The printed eſtamago is retained rather than modernized to estomago.
Munasaki receives the same anatomical meaning as Munamoto. Idem is a cross-reference to the immediately preceding definition.
Munasawagi is inner agitation or unease of the heart. Co- begins coração across the physical line boundary; the tilde placement in Perturbaçaõ is preserved.
Completes coração and gives munasawagi wo suru, experiencing inner alarm. The Portuguese verb perturbarſe is divided after Pertur-.
Completes the example as being inwardly disturbed, for instance by fear. The scan has a point after interiormente before lowercase como; that punctuation is not regularized into the OCR comma.

runs.text: Magreira de peßoa que lhe pa-

lines.note: Munasudare describes an emaciated person whose ribs or bones show. The Portuguese Magreira is retained as printed, and pa- begins parecem.

runs.text: recem os oßos. Palaura baixa & pouco

lines.note: Completes the visible-bones explanation and labels the word low-register and little used. The ligature ß in oßos is preserved.
Vſada completes pouco vſada, 'little used'. This short line is a usage qualification of Munasudare, not another definition.
Munashii means vain or fruitless; munashii shinroo is wasted effort. The scan separates Couſa vaã and does not show a comma after Vt; the tilde in vaã and the caron in xinrǒ are retained.
Translates munashii shinroo as work done in vain or wasted labour. It is the explanation of the preceding example, not a new headword.

runs.text: Adu Em vaõ, l, vaã mẽte. ¶

lines.note: Munashuu is the corresponding adverb, 'vainly' or 'in vain'. The source prints Adu without a point and separates vaã mẽte; the next expression begins with the divided Mu-.
Munashuu naru literally becoming empty is glossed as dying. This established euphemistic sense is distinct from merely doing something fruitlessly.
Katana no mune is the back or spine of a sword. The final Catana is a Japanese object name within the Portuguese gloss; Catanano mune is the standalone Japanese example.
Ie no mune is the roof ridge of a house. Capital I in Iyeno corrects OCR l, and the worn m in Cumieira corrects OCR Cunuieira.
Mune here is the breast or heart. Mune wo kogasu, literally burning the heart, introduces the emotional sense of being deeply troubled.

runs.text: triſtecerſe, ou afligirſe muito com cuedados.

lines.note: Completes En-triſtecerſe: becoming sad or greatly afflicted with cares. The enlarged scan supports cuedados, including e, rather than OCR ouedudos or an automatic modernization to cuidados.
Mune ga sawagu describes the heart's agitation or inward unease. The translation divides interiormente at the margin.

Completes the inner-agitation example, then introduces another sense of Mune: the essential or central point of something. Mune functions as a named subentry here, not as a word inside a Portuguese sentence.
Completes the 'essential point' definition and gives nanzo wo mune to suru, taking something as one's main concern or principle. The printed words and particles remain unsegmented.

runs.text: Ter algũa couſa por principal, ou eßencial.

lines.note: Translates the example as taking something to be principal or essential. The scan has eßencial, matching the previous row's noun, not OCR eſtencial.

runs.text: O aleuantar a traue da cumieira

lines.note: Mune-age is raising the ridge beam. The scan separates a traue, correcting OCR atraue; the house specification continues on the following line.
Completes the ridge-beam-raising definition with 'of the house'. The short row remains associated with Mune ague.

runs.text: Finta que ſe deita por cada caſa.

lines.note: Munebetsu is a levy imposed per house. The final t is the printed checked coda; it is not expanded to modern tsu in the transcription.
Munekado is a house's roof ridge. The example repeats the headword across the line break and describes a high-roofed house.
Munekado takaki ie ari says there was a house with a high ridge. The Portuguese cumieira is divided after cu-.
Completes the description of the house's high roof ridge. It belongs to the architectural example above, not the following bodily-pain entry.
Mune mushi, alternatively shintsuu, is glossed as stomach or chest pain. The visible space before l, is restored; these are the dictionary's historical terms, not a modern medical diagnosis.

runs.text: dos peitos, que muitas vezes vem aos Iapoẽs,

lines.note: Completes the reference to the chest and says the condition often affects Japanese people. The source reads aos, not OCR avs; Iapoẽs retains its printed tilde carrier.

runs.text: que por ventura he doença de lombrigas.

lines.note: The compilers tentatively attribute the pain to intestinal worms: por ventura means perhaps. The uncertainty belongs to their historical explanation and is not endorsed as medical advice.
Munen is anger, resentment, or regret. The example begins munen wo and continues with the verb for dispelling or venting it below.
Munen wo sanzuru is rendered as taking revenge or relieving oneself of resentment. The scan indents this continuation, correcting the provisional flush-left placement.
Completes the reference to hatred, then gives munen ni zonzuru, feeling regret or resentment. This row is also visibly indented as part of the entry.
Completes the second example as having regret or resentment about something. The worn final vowel in dalgũa is a, not OCR s; the continuation indentation is restored.
Munengari, munengaru, munengatta denotes feeling regret. The scan and the surrounding Munen family support n in Munengari rather than OCR Mumengari.

runs.text: Couſa de que ſe tem pena, ou raiua.

lines.note: Munenna qualifies something that causes regret or anger. Its adjectival ending connects it to the preceding noun, but it remains a separate printed headword.
Munenni is the adverbial derivative, printed without a fresh Portuguese gloss. Its visible indentation is preserved; no missing definition is invented.
Munensa is the nominal degree or state derivative of the same family. The scan really contains only this indented form and a point above the lower rule, not a displaced catchword.
Munetono tçuuamono denotes distinguished fighting men; the Portuguese calls them renowned soldiers. The roman head phrase and italic gloss begin a new entry at the column head.
The continuation adds that these soldiers are courageous or valiant. The conjunction and final period belong to the preceding entry, not a separate headword.

runs.text: O não ter dous, ou não

lines.note: Muni is explained by Futatçu naxi, having no second or counterpart. The Portuguese begins the literal explanation, with a visibly nasalized não at each occurrence.
Having no second is equated with Sugureta, excellence or superiority. The explanatory i, and Japanese equivalent are roman between the two italic Portuguese passages.

The gloss finishes with singularity, then gives Munino chǔxet as an example of unparalleled service. Retain the final t of the dictionary's checked-coda notation and the visible Serui- line-end division.

runs.text: ços ſingulares, ou que não ha outros taes.

lines.note: This completes Serui- / ços and explains services for which there are no others of the same kind. The phrase taes is the historical spelling, not a reason to modernize the text.
Muni muſan extends the literal counting formula: a unique thing with neither a second nor a third. Its long ſ and the new paragraph marker are visible in the scan.
The line finishes the explanation with second or third. There is no additional Japanese text after the final period at the right.
Muninjô is explained by the absence of human voices, hence solitude or silence. The end is ſi- with a printed division mark, not the OCR's ſia; the headword has a circumflex.
This completes ſi- / lencio. The upright Bup. labels the expression as Buddhist usage; its period is also kept outside the italic gloss.

runs.text: O não ter, ou não ſaber al-

lines.note: Munô and Nô naxi express lack of an art or skill. The final visible letters are al- before gũa on the next line, so the lost OCR l is restored rather than expanding the nasal abbreviation.
The continuation completes algũa arte and introduces Munôna fito, an unskilled person. The nasal mark remains on u, and the example is roman while its translation is italic.
The translation describes a person without arts and abilities. These are the completions of the example above, not an additional sense introduced on this row.
Munôna and munôxa are alternative descriptions of a person lacking accomplishments. The scan supports the doubled-s ligature in Peßoa and the two circumflex-marked Japanese forms.
The continuation reads habilidades, with an i after the first l as well as after b. Restoring the OCR omission completes the same arts-and-abilities formula seen two lines above.
Munzuto and muzuto are adverbial variants describing a forceful grip. Adu. is italic apparatus, and the printed a- at the right begins apertar on the following row.

runs.text: pertar na mão, ou pegar fortemente. Vt,

lines.note: The definition is gripping in the hand or taking hold firmly. The example begins with wholly roman Mũ; there is no visible terminal hyphen, and its nasal abbreviation is not expanded.
This completes Mũ / zuto ximuru, translated as gripping in this manner. The physically divided Japanese example is kept on its two printed rows.
Muzuto cunde illustrates grappling or taking hold with the hands. The paragraph mark introduces an additional example rather than a new headword.
The continuation makes the forceful wrestling sense explicit. Retain the historical aferrando and the visible cedilla in força.
Muqe, uru, eta supplies the principal forms for turning something. The example contrasts turning the front or face with turning the back; the list and its punctuation remain roman.

runs.text: Virar o roſto, ou as cor

lines.note: The example completes the action of turning one's face or back. The minute damaged mark after co at the right is r-like; the aligned cor / ſtas is retained as a nonblocking uncertainty rather than regularized to costas or replaced by an inferred hyphen.

The initial ſtas completes the preceding reference to the back, despite the uncertain extra r-like impression at that line's edge. Dochiye muqete iquca asks in which direction someone is going; Pera begins its translation.

runs.text: que parte ides dirigido? ¶ Item, Tirarſe

lines.note: The question is completed as asking the direction of travel. Item then opens the distinct peeling-off sense of the same printed verb entry.
The objects that come off are skin, bark, and similar coverings. Yubino cauaga mu- starts the example in which the skin of a finger has peeled off; the Japanese terminal hyphen is visible.

runs.text: Tirouſe a pelle do dedo. i, Esfolou

lines.note: Completing mu- / qeta, the gloss says the skin came off the finger and restates this as being skinned. The explanatory i, is part of the italic Portuguese apparatus, and no hyphen is supplied after Esfolou.
The first ſe completes Esfolou / ſe; Qino cauaga muqeta then applies the same verb to a tree's bark. Keeping the physical division prevents the two examples from being accidentally joined.
This finishes the translation: the bark came off the tree. Historical aruore is preserved rather than modernizing its consonant spelling.

Muqen is illustrated by Muqengigocu, the hell of uninterrupted punishment. Enlargement separates a worn round o between the second g and c; the aligned example is retained rather than deleting that faint vowel or treating its ink disturbance as e.

runs.text: lugar de tormentos onde ſem ceßar ſão atormẽ

lines.note: The line describes a place of torments in which the damned are continually afflicted. The tilde in atormẽ is a printed abbreviation and is retained without adding a terminal hyphen.
This completes atormẽ / tados and identifies the sufferers as the damned. The final upright S. is the written-usage label, distinct from the italic explanation.
This Muqi entry means stripping off a covering. Cono- begins the example about removing the skin of a fruit; its visible hyphen belongs to the printed line division.

The example completes Cono- / mino and says to remove a fruit's skin. The q in muqu is worn but retains a descender; the Portuguese supplies the synonymous verb eſ- / brugar without changing the physical division.
Brugar completes the preceding divided verb, with fruita as its object. The historical spelling and single physical continuation line are preserved.
This separate homographic Muqi entry means to vomit, not to peel or turn. The final B. is upright and marks low or vulgar usage according to the dictionary's key.
The noun Muqi is glossed as manner or mode, then illustrated by the disposition of a house. The paragraph and Cono iye- belong to the same entry.
The house example says its arrangement is good, rendered as being well laid out. The visible grave accent in eſtà and the lança- division are retained.
This completes lança- / da and adds traçada, planned or arranged. It is an alternative Portuguese rendering of the house example rather than a new Japanese phrase.
A further Muqi verb entry means to turn or position oneself facing something. The principal forms are kept distinct from the identically spelled peeling and vomiting entries above.

runs.text: Cono iye qitaye muita, l, qitamuqi

lines.note: Cono iye qitaye muita and qitamuqi are alternative ways to describe a house facing north. The sentence remains incomplete here and ends with gia on the next physical row.

runs.text: Esta caſa eſtà lançada ao norte. ¶

lines.note: Gia finishes the preceding Japanese statement, followed by its north-facing-house translation. The new Co- example begins at the right; this row is visibly a continuation and its indentation has been restored.

runs.text: Ponde vos de fronte, ou vi-

lines.note: Co- / chiye muqe is an instruction to face this way. The indented placement and the Portuguese vi- division both continue the existing entry rather than starting a headword.
The continuation finishes vi- / rai and specifies turning toward here. The grave accent in cà is printed, and the missing continuation indentation is restored.

The scan reads Muqiai, with the i on each side of a, not the OCR's truncated Muqa. The reciprocal verb and Portuguese gloss describe being turned toward one another; both following forms carry carons.

Muqiqe is glossed as an illness causing vomiting, consistent with its relation to the vomiting verb above. The worn headword is retained as read, and the upright X. marks regional usage rather than part of the Portuguese sentence.
Muquan and Qu an naxi denote lack of office or rank. The Portuguese appears as Se dignidade without a recoverable nasal mark; retain that graphic reading rather than silently supplying m or a tilde.
Mu- / quan mu-ina fito describes a person without rank or office. The nasal abbreviations in Homẽ and nẽ are retained, and this example continuation is indented to match the scan.
This completes the description with office or charge. It is an indented body continuation; the separate far-right Mura is a catchword anticipating the next page, not part of this translation.
